title: The Admiral Who Never Lost - Yi Sun-sin

shots.line: In 1597, a Korean admiral wrote to his king.
The navy had just been destroyed.
shots.scene: Burning Korean warships on a blood-red sea

shots.line: Almost every ship was gone. And he wrote:
shots.scene: An empty sea; one lonely ship on the horizon

shots.line: "I still have twelve ships."
shots.scene: The letter: "I still have twelve ships."

shots.line: Weeks later, with thirteen ships, he faced a Japanese fleet of more than a hundred and thirty.
shots.scene: 13 red Korean ships vs 133 Japanese ships, counted out

shots.line: He didn't lose a single one.
shots.scene: 3D: Korean line faces the Japanese fleet

shots.line: His name was Yi Sun-sin.
shots.scene: Profile silhouette of Yi Sun-sin before a red sun

shots.line: By the usual count, he fought around twenty-three naval battles, and never lost one.
And unlike most legends, we don't have to take anyone's word for it.
He wrote it down himself.
This is the lore behind Admiral Yi Sun-sin.
shots.scene: Ransom-note title over a ghost turtle ship

shots.line: He was born in 1545, in Seoul, into a noble family that had fallen on hard times.
He didn't start out as a sailor.
shots.scene: A warship at sea, crossed out

shots.line: He started out as a soldier.
shots.scene: Young Yi with a spear, pines, red sun

shots.line: At twenty-seven, he took Korea's military service exam.
Halfway through the horseback test, his horse threw him, and he broke his leg.
The story goes that he got up, stripped bark from a willow tree, splinted his own leg,
shots.scene: He kneels by a willow, stripping bark

shots.line: and finished the test.
shots.scene: Splinted, he limps on to finish the test

shots.line: He still failed.
Four years later, he tried again, and passed.
His early career was anything but glorious.
shots.scene: A lonely soldier on a frontier ridge at dusk

shots.line: He was posted to remote frontiers.
shots.scene: Map: posted to the remote northern frontier

shots.line: He made enemies by refusing to do favors for powerful officials.
In 1587, after a raid on the northern border,
shots.scene: A border raid at dusk, arrows in the air

shots.line: he was blamed for the losses, stripped of his rank, and made to serve as a common soldier.
shots.scene: Stripped of rank: Yi kneels as an official points

shots.line: He worked his way back.
shots.scene: He walks back toward the rising sun

shots.line: And in 1591, a friend in the government got him an unlikely job:
shots.scene: An official hands him a commission scroll

shots.line: commander of the navy in Jeolla, Korea's southwest province.
The timing was perfect.
shots.scene: Calm water, red sails at anchor

shots.line: Because across the sea, Japan had just been unified after a century of civil war,
under a warlord named Toyotomi Hideyoshi.
And Hideyoshi wanted more.
He planned to march through Korea and conquer China.
shots.scene: Map: the plan, Japan → Korea → China

shots.line: Yi seemed to sense what was coming.
He trained his sailors, stockpiled supplies,
shots.scene: Yi drills his sailors on deck

shots.line: and rebuilt an old Korean design: the turtle ship.
A warship covered with a roof, studded with sharp spikes so no one could board it,
shots.scene: The turtle ship: roof and spikes

shots.line: with cannons on every side and a dragon's head at the bow that could pour out smoke.
shots.scene: Cannons and a smoking dragon head

shots.line: According to his diary, he was test-firing its cannons just days before the invasion began.
shots.scene: His diary: cannon test days before the war

params.title: WAR DIARY · SPRING 1592
params.quote: Cannon test. Days before the war.

shots.line: In the spring of 1592, Japan invaded with an army of more than one hundred and fifty thousand men, landing at Busan.
shots.scene: 3D: a vast Japanese armada nears Busan

shots.line: They were veterans of a hundred years of war, armed with muskets.
shots.scene: Rows of samurai: veterans of 100 years of war

shots.line: Korea's army collapsed.
Seoul fell in less than three weeks.
shots.scene: Map: Busan to Seoul in under three weeks

shots.line: The king fled north.
On land, Korea was losing everything.
At sea, it was a different story.
shots.scene: 3D: but at sea, Yi's fleet advances

shots.line: Yi's fleet sailed out and caught Japanese ships at Okpo. He won.
Then at Sacheon, he sent the turtle ship into battle for the first time.
shots.scene: Map: Sacheon, the turtle ship sails

shots.line: It smashed straight into the Japanese line, and musket fire couldn't stop it.
shots.scene: The turtle ship rams the Japanese line through musket smoke

shots.line: Yi himself was shot in the shoulder.
shots.scene: On deck, Yi is struck in the shoulder

shots.line: He kept fighting, and won again. Then again. And again.
shots.scene: Map: win, win, win along the coast

shots.line: Then came Hansan Island.
Yi sent a few ships to provoke a large Japanese fleet, then turned and fled into open water.
shots.scene: Map: bait ships flee to open water

shots.line: The Japanese chased them.
And that's when Yi's whole fleet swung around into a giant half-moon,
shots.scene: Map: the fleet swings into a half-moon

shots.line: the crane wing formation, and closed around them.
Most of a Japanese fleet of more than seventy ships was destroyed or captured.
It was a turning point of the war.
Japan's army depended on supplies by sea, and Yi had cut the road.
Their advance in the north stalled.
shots.scene: Map: the advance stalls at Pyongyang

shots.line: So you'd think Korea treated him as a hero.
Instead, it nearly killed him.
shots.scene: The palace looms huge over a tiny Yi

shots.line: Yi's rivals at court were jealous.
And the Japanese fed false intelligence to the Korean government through a double agent:
shots.scene: A double agent passes false intelligence

shots.line: a Japanese fleet would be crossing at a certain spot, and Yi should attack it there.
Yi suspected a trap and refused to sail.
The king saw it as disobedience.
In 1597, Yi Sun-sin was arrested,
dragged to the capital in chains, and tortured.
shots.scene: Dragged to the capital in chains

shots.line: He came close to being executed.
shots.scene: Kneeling, a guard behind him: close to execution

shots.line: Instead, for the second time in his life, he was stripped of his rank and sent to serve as a common soldier.
shots.scene: A common soldier again, in the ranks

shots.line: His replacement was his rival, an admiral named Won Gyun.
Within months, Won Gyun led the fleet straight into a Japanese ambush at Chilcheollyang.
The Korean navy was wiped out. Won Gyun was killed.
Only about a dozen ships escaped.
The king had no choice. He brought Yi back.
And he suggested that maybe Yi should give up on the navy, and fight on land instead.
shots.scene: The king points inland: "Fight on land"

shots.line: Yi's reply became one of the most famous lines in Korean history:
"I still have twelve ships."
As long as I am alive, he wrote, the enemy will not dare to look down on us.
One more ship was found. That made thirteen.
In October 1597, a Japanese fleet of more than a hundred and thirty warships came through the Myeongnyang Strait,
a narrow channel with one of the strongest tidal currents in Korea. Yi was waiting.
The night before, he told his officers:
shots.scene: Night on deck: Yi addresses his officers

shots.line: "Those who seek death shall live.
Those who seek life shall die."

labels.str: THOSE WHO SEEK LIFE SHALL DIE."

shots.line: When the battle began, the other Korean captains hesitated and hung back.
shots.scene: Yi's ship ahead; the others hang back

shots.line: For a while, Yi's flagship fought almost alone, against wave after wave of enemy ships.
shots.scene: 3D: the flagship alone against wave after wave

shots.line: Then the others rejoined.
And then the current turned.
The Japanese ships, packed into the narrow strait, were pushed back into each other.
shots.scene: 3D: Japanese ships pushed back into each other

shots.line: By the end of the day, around thirty Japanese warships had been destroyed.
shots.scene: Japanese warships burn in the strait

shots.line: Yi did not lose a single ship.
It was one of the most lopsided naval victories ever recorded.
And it came at a terrible price.
Weeks later, in revenge,
Japanese soldiers killed Yi's youngest son.
shots.scene: His son fades into the light

shots.line: In his diary, Yi wrote that he wanted to die, but had to go on living for his men.
In 1598, Hideyoshi died, and the Japanese began pulling out of Korea.
shots.scene: Map: the Japanese retreat toward home

shots.line: Yi wasn't going to let them leave easily.
In December, alongside a Chinese fleet, he attacked the retreating Japanese at Noryang.
shots.scene: Map: Joseon and Ming fleets strike at Noryang

shots.line: The battle raged through the night.
shots.scene: 3D: battle through the night, ships burning

shots.line: As dawn came, Yi was on the deck of his flagship,
shots.scene: Dawn on the flagship deck; the war drum

shots.line: urging his men on with the war drum, when a bullet struck him.
shots.scene: Beating the drum — a bullet strikes him

shots.line: His last words, according to the records, were:
"The battle is at its height.
Do not announce my death."
His nephew hid his body, took up the drum, and kept beating it.
shots.scene: His nephew takes up the drum

shots.line: The fleet fought on, never knowing their admiral was gone. Noryang was a victory.
shots.scene: 3D: the fleet fights on to victory

shots.line: His last one.
So, is the streak real?
The number twenty-three depends on how you count.
Some of those were small clashes, and historians argue about where one battle ends and the next begins.
shots.scene: Map: many small clashes along the coast

shots.line: But here's what makes Yi different from almost every other undefeated legend: the evidence.
He kept a war diary for most of the seven-year war.
Today it's recognized by UNESCO as part of the Memory of the World.
Together with the Korean court records, it gives us his battles,
his doubts, his illnesses, and his grief, in his own hand.
By every count, he never lost a battle he commanded.
shots.scene: Never lost a battle he commanded

shots.line: He was jailed by his own king, tortured,
demoted twice, lost his son, and kept winning anyway.
shots.scene: He walks on, through it all

shots.line: Thirteen ships against more than a hundred and thirty.
Twenty-three battles. Zero defeats.
And a man who, even in death,
refused to let his side stop fighting.
